Mr. Speakei, before the Orders of the Day are called, I desire, by way of personal explanation, to bring to the attention of the House a speech which is reported in 1 Hansard ' of June 10 as having been made by the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes). The hon. member, speaking of the 2nd Dragoons in the Niagara peninsula, in connection with alleged political interference in militia matters, is reported as having said :
. An officer second in command, not yet qualified to command, communicated with the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German), and he, in language more befitting Carnal street, Buffalo, than an hon. member in this House, stated that Lord Dundonald would be taught that he had no power to give the extension. I shall give the story, and then we shall see whether the facts bear it out or not. He made the statement that there would be no extension -of command, and the notice which Lord Dundonald - had given was cancelled.
Further down he said :
I have not said that the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) wrote or spoke to the minister, but I have stated that the hon. member for Welland stated that in his county.
Now, Sir, I am not aware what sort of language is peculiarly fitted for Canal street, Buffalo. Evidently the hon. member does, possibly from experience. But I do say that no officer, second in command or otherwise, of the 2nd Dragoons asked me at any time to interfere to prevent Colonel Gregory from getting an extension of his command. I at no time spoke to the minister or to any officer of the department suggesting that Colonel Gregory should not get an extension, or that any recommendation that should be made for him to have an extension should be cancelled. During the last winter i had the honour of dining with Colonel Gregory and other officers of the 2nd Dragoons at St. Catharines. My hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) also was present. On that occasion Colonel Gregory stated that he had been recommended for an extension of his

term of command. I had the honour and pleasure then of congratulating him upon that fact, and never at any time did I suggest that he should not get or receive that extension. The statement that I said that Lord Dundonald would be taught that he had no power to give the extension is absolutely and unequivocally untrue. I never made such a remark ; X never made any remark which, by any tortuous construction, could be so interpreted ; and I defy the hon. member to bring any individual who will suggest that I ever made any remark that could possibly be interpreted in that way, 1 am inclined to think that it has been evolved from the hon. member's own vivid imagination.	_

Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to draw the attention of the government to the serious state of affairs among the crude oil producers in the counties of Lambton, Essex, Kent, Elgin and Middlesex. When the government brought down their tariff resolutions they do not seem to have made any provision for paying the crude oil producers their bounty. The crude oil is gathered in tank wagons and shipped in pipe lines to the receiving station. The crude producer takes receipts for the oil as he delivers it, and receives payment for the receipts from the Standard Oil Company or from 'the independent refiner. For several days they have been receiving only $1.62 a barrel. Previously they received $2.09 a barrel. What I am anxious to know is how these men are going to get their bounty money. There are hundreds of them scattered throughout those counties, who have been receiving payment from the refiners at the $1.62 rate. I would like the Finance Minister to explain how these men are likely to get their money, and how soon.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry that I cannot give the information which the hon. gentleman wants, nor is it possible for anybody to give it. The payment of a bounty requires an Act of this parliament. Notice of motion has been given, and in due course that notice of motion will come forward. If it is found to be in any way defective, we will, of course have it rectified to make it serve the purpose announced. It will then be crystallized into an Act of parliament, and that Act, as usual, will take effect from the date on which the announcement was made. Until that Act passes we shall not be in a position to pay a cent of bounty to any one. As to the details which the hon. gentleman mentions, these have been brought to the attention of the government by several gentlemen. To these and other questions relating to the tariff we shall give careful, attention, and when the resolutions come up to be dealt with, we shall endeavour to make them as Mr. GERMAN.
satisfactory as possible. But it is not possible at present to state to my bon. friend more than I have now said.

Seeing that it is customary that tariffs, when they are changed, are brought into effect on a date when no inconvenience would be caused to any one, had the Minister of Finance, in his statement with reference to the tariff on oil, stated that it would come into effect on the 1st of July, I feel satisfied that we should have had very little trouble, and the government would have had time to investigate the matter. But it seems to me that the government of this country were anxious to make a sort of fireworks display-

Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called, I have a matter of some importance to bring up respecting one of the most important industries of this country, namely, the fishing industry, and more particularly a very important branch of it carried on in Prince Edward Island-the lobster fisheries. Early in April I received a communication from some people at the eastern end of Prince Edward Island, accompanied by a petition signed by ten or fifteen of the most important business people in King's county, protesting against certain abuses of the lobster regulations that had taken place during the

last two years. I read a copy of the petition which was forwarded.
Does the bon. gentleman intend to move the adjournment ?
If necessary I shall do so. The matter is of such importance that I thought possibly the motion would not be necessary.
It may lead to debate and it would be more in order for the hon. gentleman to make a motion.

I shall do so. This is the petition :
Souris, April 11th, 1904.
Hon. Raymond Prgfontaine,
Minister of Marine and Fisheries,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-The undersigned lobster packers of Prince Edward Island wish to call your attention to the following abuse of the granting of licenses for packing lobsters on Prince Edward Island
We were given to understand that, acting under an Order in Council passed some time since, no more fishing licenses would he granted upon Prince Edward Island.
Last season, through the influence of Mr. J. J Hughes, M.P., for this county, a fishing license for packing lobsters was granted to Mr. McEachern, of Black Bush, thereby opening a new factory between that of Mr. A. D. Mc-Isaac and Messrs. Matthew and McLean-.
This season we understand that Mr. Hughes has gone into partnership with Mr. John Ryan, of Priest Pond, and is securing for him another license for packing lobsters between Matthew's and McLean's factory and Donald Leslie's, Campbell's Cove.
We consider this action on the part of the department very unfair, and we should either have licenses for every person that asked for them for packing lobsters, or else the Order in Council should be adhered to.
Before these latter licenses were granted, there were five factories from Black Bush to East Point in a distance of eighteen miles, and if these two factories are allowed to run. it will mean seven factories in a distance of eighteen miles on a straight shore.
We trust, therefore, that your department will see fit not to grant any license to Mr. Ryan, and that the license of Mr. McEachern will be cancelled, otherwise that all fishermen applying for licenses for packing shall he granted to them.
We remain, truly yours,
Location Factories- East Point.
Bayfield & North Lake Campbell's Cove,
Bay Fortune, Annandale,
St. Peter's Harbour, Black Bush, Georgetown, Georgetown,
C. H. S. STERNS. .MATTHEW & McLEAN, DONALD. C. LESLIE, JAS. W. DINGWELL, EDWIN McFARLANE. H,D. McEWBN,

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.

speechtext:
This petition is signed irrespective of party allegiance. A number of those who signed it are strong supporters of the
present administration. It is simply a protest, as it says, against an Order in Council, but I afterwards found there was no Order in Council, but that the government was simply following out certain lines of policy respecting this industry. The parties who forwarded this petition thought the matter of such grave importance to the- lobster industry that they wired me that they were prepared to present the petition.in person if that were necessary. I immediately communicated with the department, and received the following letter from the deputy minister :
Ottawa, April 15th, 1904.
Sir,-In reply to your letter of to-day's date, addressed to Mr. Venning, I have much pleasure in inclosing copy of the lobster fishery regulations at present in force in the Dominion.
Touching your inquiry with regard to the establishment of new caneries, I may say that owing to the ever increasing number of lobster canneries along the Atlantic shores of Canada, it has been found necessary, in the interest of fishermen as well as of the fishery, to curtail as much as possible the issue of new licenses, particularly in localities where the number of lobster canneries has reached the maximum of what the fishery will stand, and with this end in view, the department has adopted the policy of refusing applications for new canneries, and in this connection, applications for licenses to reopen canneries which have not been operated for period of two years, are regarded as additional ones.
I am, sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) F. GOURDEAU, Deputy ^Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
A. A. Lefurgey, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons.
I was not quite satisfied and thought it my duty to push the matter further. The deputy minister stated that when they thought there were a sufficient number of lobster canneries in operation along a certain line of the coast it was the policy of the government not to grant new applications. I had a map of the district made, and found that within a space of souse twenty miles there were seven factories in operation, and I considered that the establishment of any new factories along that coast was not justified. I therefore interviewed the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and he said he would look into the case and send me a communication. On the 22nd April I received the following communication from the minister :
Office of -the Minister of Marine and Fisheries of Canada,
Ottawa, April 22nd, 1904. gir>-in view of the policy of the deportment to prevent as much as possible an undue increase in the number of lobster canneries on the Atlantic coasts, by placing necessary restraint upon -their multiplication, as well in the interests of 'the canners themselves as in that of the preservation of the fishery, which could

not but inure to the benefit of the fishermen, it became necessary to adopt measures to that and in carrying out a careful administranor. of provident rules and regulations in this regard.
It was therefore decided to limit the licenses where it was regarded that the number reasonably allowable, compatible with profitable results and rational protection, had been reached, hence, it was deemed expedient, under such condition®, to, as much as could be, restrict the business to canneries already established, and incidentally to encourage and turn the attention of the operators to the export of live lobsters, a branch of the industry which has been shown to be capable of producing very much larger returns to all concerned.
In dealing with applications for licenses for lobster canneries, the issue of new licenses has been avoided, unless peculiar and exceptional conditions obtain, and in the category of new applications is included requests for the reopening of disused canneries in which operations have been closed for a period of two years and over.
I believe I need scarcely assure you that in adopting such a policy the department was solely actuated by a desire to so adjust the interests involved as to effect as much protection as possible consistent with a minimum amount of restriction to an established and legitimate industry, but I am sure you will readily appreciate the difficulties which necessarily surround all such attempts, when dealing with fishing interests, which are so susceptible to varying conditions.
To that part of the letter I do not think any one can take exception otherwise than that it leaves too much latitude to ministers, which may lead to abuse, as in this case. That is the definite policy of the government-not brought down in an Order in Council, but just as rigid-and should be just as strictly enforced as an Order in Council would be, to prevent illegal fishing on the Atlantic coast with regard to lobsters. He goes on :
In explanation of the authorization of two new lobster canning licenses on the eastern coast of Prince Edward Island, I may say that after carefully considering urgent representations, I recognized the fact th^t under the circumstances, the fishermen of the particular locality, were placed at a great disadvantage by reason of a practical monopoly by lobster packers, who fixed the prices to be paid for the lobsters and compelled the fishermen to supply them on their terms.
The fishermen then appealed for authority to pack the lobsters actually caught by them, as a remedy against being coerced to dispose of them at the packers' own prices, and with some reluctance, in the light of the general policy above outlined, I consented to grant such relief ; but only on condition that they should organize themselves into a proper company, satisfactory to the department, for such specific purpose, when two licenses, and two only would issue.
The effect of this concession, you will observe, in no way operates to increase the number of lobsters actually taken in the locality, nor does it increase the number actually packed there ; but merely enables certain fishermen to themselves put up their own catch, instead of selling it to the packers, on terms dictated by the purchasers.	-

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext:
Hence, as the primary object of the regulations is to conserve the lobster fishery for all parties concerned, it would seem that in this special case, the interest of the fishermen have been accommodated without involving any unnecessary increase to the packing or catching power of the canneries or fishermen of the district.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) R. A. PREFONTAINE.
A. A. Lefurgey, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons.
This was the communication I received from the Minister of Marine, and as I Was not satisfied that the hon. minister had made out a case justifying such a departure from an avowed policy, and as I had been down to Prince Edward Island and made some inquiry into the matter, I was obliged to put several questions on the order paper. On April 28th, I put certain questions to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries on this subject :
1.	Have any new licenses been granted for the establishment of any new lobster canneries in Prince Edward Island, other than the two mentioned in an official letter of the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, dated April 22nd, 1904 ?
To this the minister answered, * No. '
2.	If so, what is the location of the same, and the names of the persons to whom granted ?
Answered above.
3.	What applications have been received for reopening of the canneries closed for two years, and the names and locations of same ?
3.	William Moore, Wood Islands ; William Sudsbury, Sea View ; William Adams, Sea View ; John T. McKay, Sea View ; Arnold Malone, Miseouehe.
I knew of several of these cases, these being men wdio had been engaged in the business of lobster packing. I knew their applications had been in, and they had been endeavouring for some time to reopen canneries that had been running before. But it was evident from the answer of the minister that these men, who had been engaged in the business of lobster packing and whose livelihood depended on the business, had not been allowed to reopen in these places even though the lobster packers there were not within twenty-five per cent of what they were along the eastern shore of King's county, where they had granted two new licenses.
4.	Have any been granted ; and if so, what are the names and localities ? If not, is it the intention of the government to reopen any of these ?
4. No license have been issued for any of the canneries referred to in the answer to question No. 3.	.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I considered in view of the knowledge I already had of these cases, and of the knowledge I gained on my trip to Prince Edward Island a month ago, that there was a manifest injustice and unfairness in the action of the Minister of Mar-

ine in refusing to open these factories when he allowed the opening of two new lobster factories in the part of the Island to which the petition refers. On the same day I asked another series of questions :
Referring to an official letter from the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, dated April 22nd, 1904, the following statement appears :-* In explanation of the authorization of two new lobster-canning licenses on the eastern coast of Prince Edward Island, I may say that, after carefully considering urgent representations, I recognize the fact that under the circumstances the fishermen of this particular locality were placed at a great disadvantage by reason of a practical monopoly b'y lobster packers, who fixed the prices to be paid for the lobsters, and compelled the fishermen to supply them on their terms.
That was the passage I read from the letter of the Minister of Marine, and I was anxious to know, in view of that appearing as the reason for the establishment of these two lobster factories where he had received his information. Therefore, in view of the expressions 'practical monopoly' and ' urgent representation, ' I asked also :
1.	What is the usual arrangement between lobster fishermen and packers with regard to prices paid and basis of payment ?
2.	Do not packers arrange with fishermen at stated prices for lobsters delivered at factory ?
3.	What was the price paid by the lobster packers in the section referred to in above letter of April 22nd, 1904, during the season the monopoly was complained of ?
4.	What were the average prices paid in other parts of Prince Edward Island during the same season ?
6.	What are the names of the fishermen who applied for authority to pack in this section ?
7.	What are the names of the fishermen who were being coerced to dispose of their lobsters at the packers' own price ?
Now, this was a series of questions right in line with tbe paragraph I quoted from the minister's own letter. Therefore, I could not understand it when the minister replied to these questions that he had no information in the department, although it must have been on the basis of information in the department that he established two new lobster canneries. Yet, in answer to every one of these questions, without some information as to the subject of which neither he nor his department could have acted, he replied that he had no information in the department ;-no information as to the fishermen who complained of this monopoly ; no information as to the prices that were paid In that locality that would create a monopoly ; no information as to the prices paid in other parts of Prince Edward Island that he could compare with the prices paid there that he might judge whether monopoly prices were paid or not. When I was on the Island, I took the trouble to inquire as to the prices paid in the locality complained of and in other places in Prince Edward Island, and I found that the prices
paid to lobster fishermen were practically the same as elsewhere and that the fishermen of that locality were earning as much money in the season as most of the other lobster fishermen on Prince Edward Island. Now, I asked him two other questions :
Where are the two factories mentioned In said letter of April 22nd, 1904, on the eastern coast of Prince Edward Island located or to be located ?
The answer to this was :
Only one license applied for at Priest's Point.
He referred to two in his letter, but one had been established last year and, the petition called for the cancelling of that license. The last question was :
What are the names of the parties to whom said two licenses mentioned in said letter of April 22nd, 1904, were or are to be granted ?
And the answer was :
One license to Hughes & Ryan.
In face of the minister's letter that there was a monopoly among the lobster packers in that section of the country, and that the minister with great reluctance was departing from the avowed policy of the government not to establish any new factories nor to reopen any old ones, and In view of his words that he was granting these licenses to open two new factories only on the application of a certain number of fishermen formed into a company to carry on this fishery, it seems strange to find a license granted to a supporter of the government in this House. The minister was not justified in allowflig political influences to prevail or to prostitute the avowed policy of the government in relation to the lobster fishery in Prince Edward Island. I may say that the lobster fishery of Prince Edward Island, as along almost the whole Atlantic coast-in contradistinction to most of the other fisheries in Canada has not been progressing ; and the utmost care must be exercised in carrying out any policy that the government sees fit to adopt with regard to that fishery. A commission has been appointed and has been working on the problem of protecting the lobster fisheries for some years. In view of this serious state of affairs in the lobster business in Prince Edward Island, it seems clear that there has been a grave violation of the policy of the government, and, as I have pointed out, the minister has not seen fit to justifiy his case-for he declared that he had no information in the department that there was a monopoly existing. Therefore, he has clearly not justified his action in allowing an hon. member of this House to use his position to secure a license for himself in a locality which was already well supplied with lobster canneries, and which I can show, from Information I have gained,
4GT5

was not suffering from a monopoly, but in which the fishermen were being treated as well as anywhere else in Prince Edward Island. No complaint has been made of any of the lobster packers named in this petition, and those who signed the petition are employing the same number of men right along, and the hon. minister in putting for* ward such a plea as he did in the last part of his letter, in saying that the establishment of another factory would not tend to increase the number of lobsters caught and cause the employment of any more men along that shore is an absolute absurdity, because these same people are employing the same number of hands in that locality as they employed regularly for a number of years past, and the other factory is just filling in by an addition of five to eight boats a factory. The minister will see that the principle laid down in his department is violated by an action which, upon the face of it, bears the impress of a political favour to a member of this House, and he is putting the fishermen in that locality in a worse position than they were before, because all of this ground had to be allotted again amongst an added number of fishermen. The department by the establishment of two new factories, along a shore line where there were already sufficient, has cut off the catch of the men, whom he professes to be looking after.
From the information I have gained I find that from Cow River to East Point there were six factories almost evenly distributed, and that in all these factories so far as I can learn the prices to be paid to fishermen were arranged between the fishermen and the packers early in the season before any fishing commenced, so that the fishermen always knew the price they were to receive before they put their hands to a trap, and if they were not satisfied with the price they always had the option, and had plenty of "time to make arrangements with other packers in any other part of Prince Edward Island.

I am coming to that if my hon. friend will wait. As regards the statement that the fishermen ever asked for permission to pack their own lobsters, and that tnis permission was to be granted by the establishment of a proper company satisfactory to the government, the facts are that Mr. Hughes, M.P., formed a partnership with Mr. John Ryan, of Priest Pond, and this company is now employing four-boats to fish the ground formerly occupied by one. They have now in this locality three factories all running full blast on the ground formerly occupied by one, so you can readily understand that the protection meant to be given to the fishermen of the locality was very poorly afforded when the Min-Mr. LEFURGEY.
ister of Marine and Fisheries allowad two factories to be established on the ground formerly occupied by one. I asked several questions of different lobster packers in tlie locality as to whether any complaints had been made to them at any time during the past four or five years. They said that they had been packing lobsters for some 25 years past, and during all that time any fisherman or any one else was perfectly free under the Conservative government to establish as many factories as they pleased, but in all that time not one of their fishermen ever thought of establishing a factory. Under me Conservative policy of allowing any one to establish factories none of these fishermen wanted to establish factories. The number of factories then varied as the catch varied during different seasons. They also say that these fishermen had been with them during almost the whole period they had been operating along this coast. The coast line, they say, is fairly straight, and they have always divided the ground fished by the boats of different factories as defined by land marks, each fisherman operating on his own section exclusively and no one else being allowed to hinder 'him. I also inquired about this Mr. Ryan and what he had been doing. I found that he had been employed by one of the firms along this shore, I think Matthew & McLean, for quite a long time, and up to the very time he left their employment to go into partnership with J. J. Hughes, he had made no complaint to them about the price he was being paid by the people with whom he was employed. The price that has been paid along that coast has been $1.10 per 100 pounds for the fish, boarding the fishermen during the day-time, that is two meals per day, finding the traps, boats and everything that they require, giving each man as well, enough salt to salt his herring for bait and at the factories on the south side the fishermen earn from $2.50 to $2.75 per hundred pounds, the fishermen finding everything including traps, boats, &c. I wish to point out to the members of this House that the fishermen under these prices were making as much money as the average fisherman throughout Prince Edward Island. They were making from $150 to $170 per year and made more per man clear in each season by these arrangements, reserving so much ground for each 300 traps and allowing them to draw lots for positions.
I have given the House all the information I could get. I could get no more information from the Department of Marine and Fisheries than I have presented to the House and I am perfectly satisfied to leave it to the intelligence of the hon. the First Minister and the other members of this House whether the Minister of Marine, in his statement of the case as I have fairly presented it to the House, was justified in de-

parting from the avowed policy of protecting the lobster fisheries of Prince Edward Island, and in apparently using the Department of Marine and Fisheries in ordei; to satisfy a political supporter of the party opposite. This is not the only department of the government which is being misused for the purpose of satisfying political friends.
We had an? instance, only the other day where a department of the government, the Militia Department, which, possibly more than any other should be kept free from political partisanship, was most grossly misused by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), who had no connection wit'll that department, and wTho should, therefore, have not interfered with it at all. Now, we have this case in connection with the department of the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who, while professing to have an established policy and to carry it out for the protection of the fisheries, has been guilty of almost as gross an abuse as that of which the hon. Minister of Agriculture has been guilty in connection with the Department of Militia and Defence. I want to say that if it is the policy of this government that no new cannery shall be established along the Atlantic coast or along the shores of Prince Edward Island, and that no old factories shall be reopened, we want the same treatment meted out to every private individual in Prince Edward Island, who wants to undertake the establishment of a cannery along these shores and to engage in the lobster fishery. In view of the fact that in this case an important departure from the avowed policy of the government has been made, that the name of an hon. member of this House is coupled with it and that throughout the length and breadth of the land for the past three or four seasons all applications for the privilege of establishing new canneries and reopening old ones have been disregarded it seems to me that this is a plain case of prostituting the policy of the department in favour of political partisans. Mr. Speaker, I beg to move that the House do now adjourn.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Prefoutaine) is not present perhaps a wprd of explanation from me in regard to this matter may not be out of place. The hon. member for Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) is in the habit of taking up questions in this House that he does not very well understand ; in fact, I am inclined to think that if he only spoke upon the questions that he did understand he would not say so much. This is really a small matter and I am surprised that my hon. friend should have seen fit to bring it up in this House. However, as my name has been mentioned in connection with it I deem it my duty to give some explanation. In regard to the question as to whether or not 149
ai practical monopoly in the lobster canning business existed on this part of the coast I make this statement and it is a statement of fact: From a place called Black Bush, .on the north side of the island, to Souris, on the south side of the island, a distance of between forty and fifty miles. N

speechtext: Black Bush to Souris or to East Point ?

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext: Black Bush to Souris and around East Point. There were just two men interested in the canning business in that vicinity, namely, John McLean, a gentleman who will probably be my opponent in the next election, who has been nominated for that position, and his brother-in-law, Charles /Sterns. Along that particular piece of coast some few years ago there were several factories. These people whose names I have mentioned had factories there. Factories were also owned by Messrs. Fred. Morrow, C. C. Carlton and Dennis Murphy. These factories were closed and in consequence of their closure, due to the regulation of the department against granting any licenses, these two men, the brothers-in-law, had about forty miles of coast line under their own operation. There was just one man, Joseph Pope, who had a small factory that he was running on his own account and these gentlemen were so determined to allow nobody to fish but themselves that they went opposite to his factory and set their traps. To show how the fishermen were complaining, the fishermen in that locality, a few years ago, knowing that they were getting unreasonably small profits for their industry, for the hard labour they were performing, organized a delegation which came to Souris, waited upon Mr. John McLean and asked him to allow them to go into' partnership with him in the business. They catching the fish and doing nearly all the labour wished to participate to some extent in the profits of the business. They thought it would be better for^ him as well as for themselves because under ordinary circumstances the fishermen would take a greater interest in their work and have a greater interest in preserving the property. The answer of Mr. McLean to the delegation, according to my information from the fishermen themselves, was that if they were not satisfied with their position he could get other men to take their places. I wonder if, the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), who is opposed to monopolies and all that kind of thing and who is a friend of the workingman, would approve of that kind of thing.

speechtext: No, no.

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext:
Oh, yes, my hon. friend does. Under these circumstances the fishermen came to me and asked me if it was possible to get them a license to can their own catch of fish. I certainly approved of the proposition and tried to comply with the request. I think that if there are any men who ought to profit by this industry they are the men along that coast who do the labour, the men who have to do the actual work, rather than the merchants who live at other places and who have other means of making a living. 1 make that statement. I do not know whether my hon. friend opposite will agree with and endorse it or not. It is my opinion, at all events and it is the opinion of the fishermen in that locality as my hon. friend and my opponent will probably find out. I got a license under these circumstances for the McEacherns and McDonalds who formed a company last year and went into business on their own account. These men made twice as much money out of the business when they were canning for themselves as they had made before when .they were fishing and allowing other people to can their lobsters. This year Ryan, to whom my hon. friend refers, and McPhee were going to organize another company and they applied for a license to can their fish.
My esteemed friend, the gentleman who will probably be my opponent in the nest election and who has a practical monopoly of that coast line, prevailed upon McPhee to withdraw from the business and not go into partnership with Ryan. Under these circumstances Ryan was not able to proceed with the business alone, and he came to me and I agreed to go into partnership with him rather than that it should fall through. That is my connection with the matter, and I am not ashamed of it. I am not ashamed to go before the fishermen of Prince Edward Island, and the fishermen of the eastern part of King's county and explain the transaction. I understand from Ryan that he is doing well, and if there are some four boats fishing on the ground where only one fished before, he must be fishing a larger area. To show you how the friends of the hon. gentleman opposite have tried to establish a monopoly on this part of the coast Mr. J. J. HUGHES.
line, I may say that when Ryan was prepared to put out his lobster traps and rope opposite his own cannery last spring ; Mr. John McLean, who has prompted my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) to bring up this question and who has given him all the information which he possesses-although he does not very well understand it yet-

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext: I beg thfe hon. gentleman's pardon. Mr. John Maclean did not give me the information which I possess. I took particular care to get the information from reliable men from Souris and Charlottetown ; people that the hon. gentleman knows well possibly, and they gave me the information when I was down myself.

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext: I understand the question very well. Mr. McLean sent a large party of men to prevent Ryan by force from putting out his traps opposite his own factory, and Ryan was obliged to go some distance away from his own factory, because he could not raise a mob to protect him.

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext: Where were all these oppressed fishermen that they did not flock to his assistance ?

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext: Now then with regard to this petition which my hon. friend presented ; I was not present at the moment, and I do not know whether he read all the names or not.

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext: I read all the names.

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext: Was the name A. D. Mclsaac on it ?

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext: Yes. A. D. Mclsaac was on it.

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext: Well, A. D. Mclsaac told me that his name was forged to that petition, and that he felt like taking proper steps to bring the parties who forged his name to justice. I believe the name of D. C. Leslie is on that petition ?

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext: I do not recollect just now.

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext:
Well, D. C. Leslie did not write his name ; I know his handwriting and it is not his handwriting. I cannot say anything as to the other names, but these two I know of. Mr. Mclsaac who is an honest respectable man gave me that information, and that will show you what value ought be attached to the petition and to the manner of men these are who would send this petition here. It would show the kind of men they are to use my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) to present such a document into this House. So far as this fishery regulation is concerned I do not know that I altogether approve of it. In my opinion it is weak in this respect : that it limits the number of factories that may be established along the coast line, but does not limit the number of traps that may be

put in the water, and it is the traps that catch the fish and not the factories. The limitation of the number of factories without limiting the number of traps that can be put in the water would not preserve the industry. The two gentlemen who had a practical monopoly of that coast line were enabled under the present regulations to put down as many traps as they wished and consequently the issuing of these licenses to the fishermen themselves does not injure the industry. Now, these are the facts of the case, and again I regret that my hon. friend from Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) brought the matter before the House. I do not think he has gained anything by it ; I do not think his friends have gained anything and I leave the matter there, for the present.

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend from East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) brought the matter before the House for the purpose of gaining anything politically from it. He presented the matter to parliament for the reason that it concerns the public interest. As I understand it, certain regulations were made by the department limiting the number of lobster factories along the coast, and then certain exceptions were made for this locality which do not seem to have been applied throughout the island generally. Of course, it was very kind of my hon. friend (Mr. J. J. Hughes), if he has gone into this matter for motives of pure philanthropy, and I am sure we all rejoice to hear that Ryan is doing well, because if Ryan does well the hon. member (Mr. J. J. Hughes) will do well also. But, this would not seem to exactly coincide with the policy laid down in the letter from the minister. The minister says that the exceptions have been made in the case of fishermen desiring to catch lobsters, so that they may not be obliged to work for those who are engaged in the business of canning ; and he suggests that the fishermen who desire to put up the lobsters should form themselves into an association. One would have thought that if there had been a large number of oppressed fishermen, they would have formed themselves into a company as directed by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, but that does not seem to have been done. The majority of fishermen seem to be going on as they were before. I gather that one firm was formed last year consisting of Mr. Mc-Eaehern

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext: There are several McEacherns.

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext:
At all events, there was one firm formed last year consisting of two fishermen, but this year only one of the oppressed fishermen on that coast was so dissatisfied with his own condition that he went into the business and my hon. friend from King's (Mr. J. J. Hughes) very kindly came to his relief and went into the partnership with him. That would hardly seem to indicate the distressful conditions 149J
of affairs which my hon. friend (Mr. J. J. Hughes) described to the House. Of course I know nothing about the signatures to that petition, but it is said to be signed by respectable men ; men who are known in the community in which they reside as reliable men ; men whose word is to be depended upon; and my hon. friend from King's will see that if this petition really has been signed, the statements it contains would amply justify my hon. friend from Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) in bringing in to the attention of the House. In the first place, they refer to the granting of licenses in a manner which amounts to an abuse, and then they go on to say that there was a regulation of the department that no more fishing licenses would be granted upon Prince Edward Island.

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext: My hon. friend will notice that there is not one fisherman's name on that petition ; they are canners.

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext: I don't attach very much importance to that either one way or the other if they are respectably men.

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext: Their interests are the other way.

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext:
What these men set out, is that certain regulations have been made but have not been adhered to, and that the departure from these regulations can only be described as an abuse. I do not pretend to be as familiar with the facts as myjhon. friend (Mr. J. J. Hughes) I am merely drawing his attention to this for the purpose of showing that there really is something before the House for discussion. Then the petition continues :
Last season through the influence of Mr. J. J. Hughes, M.P., for this county, a fishing license for packing lobsters was granted to Mr. Mc-Eachern, of Black B-ush, thereby opening a new factory between that of Mr. A. D. Mclsaac and Messrs. Matthew and McLean.
This season we understand that Mr. Hughes has gone into partnership w!ith M!r. John Ryan, of Priest Pond, and is securing for another license for packing lobsters between Matthew & McLean's factory and Donald Leslie's, Campbell's Cove.
We consider this action on the part of the department very unfair, and we should either have licenses for every person that asks for them for packing lobsters, or else the Order in Council should be adhered to.
The point of the petition, as I understand it, is that there should be regulations and that these regulations should be adhered to, or else depart from the regulations altogether and leave the field open to every one. You should not have regulations which are broken by means of influence such as that described in the petition. The petition continues as follows :
Before these latter licenses were granted, there were five factories from Black Bush to East Point in a distance of eighteen miles, and

if these itwo factories are allowed to run, it will mean seven factories in a distance of eighteen miles on a straight shore.
We trust therefore that your department will see fit not to grant any license to Mr. Ryan, and that the license of Mr. McEachern will be cancelled-
That Is one alternative. That alternative contemplates an adherence to the regulations of the department. The other alternative is certainly a fair one, and it is as follows :
-otherwise that all fishermen applying for license for packing lobsters shall be granted.
My hon. friend cannot see anything very unfair in the two alternatives; they are perfectly plain and straightforward, and I should think in the public interest. This petition has been signed by men who purport to be lobster packers ; Mr. C. H. S. Sterns, Messrs. Matthew & McLean, Mr. Donald C. Leslie-my hon. friend, X think calls in question his signature.

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext: It is not his handwriting.

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext: It does not make any difference whether it is his handwriting or not. If he authorized any one else to write his name, it is the same as if he wrote it himself. The other names are : Mr. James W. Dingwell, Mr. Edwin Mc-Farlane, Mr. H. D. McEwen, Mr. Angus D. Mclsaac, Messrs. A. A. McDonald Bros., Mr. W. W. Jenkins. While not professing to have a very exact knowledge of the facts or the conditions with reference to the lobster fisheries in Prince Edward Island, I think, under the circumstances which have been disclosed by my hon. friend from East Prince, he was amply justified in bringing this matter before the House.

subtopic: A A. MCDONALD BROS. W W. JENKINS.
speechtext:
I would like the hon. member for King's to understand that I had no personal olrject in bringing this matter up. I do not bring matters up in the House from personal motives. The fact that the hon. member's name is unfavourably connected with a matter of so much importance to the fishing industry of Prince Edward Island is his own misfortune, and not my fault. The petition was sent to me, and I was asked to look into the matter and bring it up in this House. I have only done what the hon. member would himself do if his constituents sent him material that contained charges of such, a nature as this one. I am glad that the hon. member feels the seriousness of the position he has got himself into, and I think hon. members will agree with me that in presenting this case to the House. I did it fairly and squarely, upon the information which I had from the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the information which I gained with regard to the industry from those engaged in it in Prince Edward Island. If the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries has not given us Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
information that would justify his departure from an avowed policy, the position of the hon. member for King's is that much more serious. The hon. member for King's has apparently put himself in the position that the hon. Minister of Agriculture is in with regard to Lord Dundonald's case. He is acting for the department to his own benefit. Instead of the department acting, it is delegating its powers to people who have no right to act. and who are very likely to act from motives that are not just in line with the policy of the government. As the Minister of Agriculture made a fatal mistake in introducing politics into militia appointments, so the Minister of Marine and Fisheries had apparently made Mr. Hughes, the member for King's, his-deputy in the information he obtained in regard to this matter. The charge certainly comes home to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and it is his duty to clear himself. He has not the information in the department, and for that reason I think his action in this case was unjustified. My statements with regard to the prices paid for lobsters and the wages paid to the men were got from reliable men engaged in the fishing industry, and I gave them exactly as I got them from those people. The fact that only one fisherman is engaged in packing, of all those who were complaining of the monopoly in that part of the island, is sufficient to justify me in bringing the matter up ; and the fact that the hon. member for King's got the minister in this position, and went into partnership with one fisherman, is no justification for claiming a monopoly for the sole purpose of benefiting Mr. J. J. Hughes, M.P.

I desire to draw the attention of the Prime Minister to the unsatisfactory condition of the equipment existing in connection with the navigation of Lake Ontario near Toronto harbour. The complaint made by mariners is that they find it very difficult, especially in foggy weather, to make the harbour at the eastern entrance because of the insufficiency of the appliances there. I have received a letter from Mr. Church, the solicitor of the Lake Ontario Navigation Company, inclosing clippings from the papers of Friday last, describing the difficulties the mariners have .to contend with. These difficulties were accentuated during two or three days of last week when there was a great deal of foggy weather. The harbour could have been made if there had been sufficient fog signals and other appliances. With the permission of the House I will read a few lines taken from the * World ' of Friday last :	.
The fog nuisance, although somewhat abated yeeio:day, w-as still sufficiently in evidence to make tiouble. The steamer ' Argyle ' was the vicUtu yesterday. With a crowd of 500 on hoard, being an excursion of the Presbyterian

Church of Cobourg, she was compelled to lie for aeout forty-five minutes within half a mile of the eastern gap, there being no sound from the bell located there to indicate her bearings. It is not stretching facts to say that practically the sole topic among marine men is the absurdly inefficient equipment for giving warning during fog.
The Richelieu and Ontario, St. Catharines, and Niagara Navigation Companies are all interested in this matter, and I would ask the Prime Minister to see that steps are taken to implement the apparatus, which is insufficient at present.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What do they complain of-the insufficiency of the signals or the insufficiency of the alarm ?
The insufficiency of the alarm.

On the 30th of May last, an order of the House was passed for copies of correspondence in relation to the construction or improvement of the landing at Beaton, B.C., and also for copies of the letters of resignation of certain officers of the 9th regiment on the same day. These returns are not down yet. and I shall pass the list over to the right bon. gentleman.

I would draw the attention of the right hon. gentleman to certain correspondence between the hon. the Minister of Agriculture and Col. Smart us well as Col. Whitley, which was referred to on Friday last by the hon. minister. That correspondence, I would suggest, should be laid on the table. We should also have any departmental correspondence on the same subject, some of which has been referred to and the contents stated to the House. It would be desirable that all this should be placed before the House. Two gazettes have also been referred to and their contents commented upon. We should have them as well, and I would suggest that all other documents bearing upon the incident, in connection with which these documents were mentioned, should also be laid on the table. The government should inform the House whether or not it was understood by the colleagues of the Minister of Agriculture that the name of Dr. Pickel had been struck off without the recommendation of the General Officer Commanding and what were the reasons for striking it off. It seems to me only proper that the House should be informed whether or not that fact was brought to the attention of His Excellency when the Order in Council was presented' to him and whether or not he was informed of tl\e reason why that name had been struck out. These are suggestions of mine and it will be for
the government to take what action it may see fit. I make them in view of the duties prescribed in the statutes for the General Officer Commanding ; and I think, having regard to those regulations which have the force of a statute, that this is information which may not unreasonably be demanded by the House in ease there should be any further discussion of the unfortunate incident to which I have referred.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. colleague the Minister of Militia is not in his seat, but I have reason to believe that he is preparing correspondence for the further information of the House.

CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY. „

I would like to say that the solicitor who resides in Montreal, after this Bill was reported, made the statement that he did not understand the committee to have adopted the Bill in the form in which it is submitted to the House. House in committee on Bill (No. 80) respecting the West Canadian Collieries, Limited.-Mr. Oliver.
On section 4,

I do not know whether the attention of the government has been directed to the very comprehensive! powers included in this clause, but they are a little unusual. We have coal mining, smelting, the operation of open hearth steel plants, bridge construction, machine shops, manufacture of the products of coal, farming and stock raising, dealing in shares and securities of other concerns carrying on similar business, construction of houses, churches, schools, hospitals and other buildings-but as that is limited by the clause * for the use and benefit of workmen ' and so on, it may not be objectionable- acquiring real and personal property, easements, hydraulic properties, patent rights, plant, machinery and so on in connection with the works ; manufacture, use and supply of electricity, water, gas and electric, hydraulic compressed air or other power-it may be all right, but it seems rather comprehensive.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Bill is rather of an unusual character, because it purports to confer powers upon a company cieated under the English Act, and which remains for the future beyond our legislative control. I confess that when I first looked at it, I thought we were giving this company more extended powers than were provided for in the articles of association. But I have had the Bill examined, and I find that the powers granted are in accordance with the articles of association and are, as I am informed, identical with the powers which the company now possesses.

I do not quite understand why we need to give the company these powers if it already possesses them under its memorandum and articles of association. It seems inconvenient that we should confer upon this company the same powers conferred upon it by its articles of association, and, at the same time, we expressly stipulate that it shall be enabled to amend its constitution without reference to this parliament and in accordance with the Companies' Act of Great Britain. I have not worked out the effect of this, but it seems to me it might, lead to awkward consequences. I do not know whether my hon. friend from Alberta {Mr. Oliver) who has charge of the Bill has communicated with the promoters on that point, but it seems to me a little dangerous to give to companies differing powers derived from a double source. In my own province of Nova Scotia we have had some companies which were constituted by the Act of the legislature of Nova Scotia and which, when they wanted wider powers, secured charters from the government of Canada. If there is the slightest variation in the powers granted by the two different authorities, it is exceedingly difficult to tell what the precise powers are. I think the promoters should be careful, in their own interest, to see how far this goes. You have perfectly plain sailing if you do not attempt to give powers here that are not contained in the company's memorandums and articles of association. But if you vary from that, you are almost sure to get into trouble.
What is done in the case of subsection (f) ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The words ' and the business of general merchants,' are struck out by the committee.

It seems to me that the hon. leader of the opposition is right in suggesting that this is rather dangerous legislation. We are giving powers in this Bill that we are denying every day to Canadian companies-I think there is no doubt about that. It is, in effect, a suggestion to promoters who desire to get larger powers, and cannot get them from this parliament, to become incorporated under the English

Act, and then, when they come here we merely pass in review, as it were, the powers they have received, giving them by confirmation powers that we would not give in the initiative. Of course, there may be a great deal of this legislation in Canada, but this is a very striking instance of our giving exceedingly broad powers ; and, as the leader of the opposition says it is rather confounding matters to have this joint or confirmatory legislation.

It seems to be rather absurd to give to a colliery company power to become a stock-raising concern. We are striking out the words that give them the power of going into the business of general merchants, but it seems to me it would be more reasonable to give them power to do business as merchants than to go into stock-raising, for they might want to do business in connection with carrying on their collieries. I fail to see why they want powers for stock-raising.

They own large areas of land in the western country and to use that land they require these powers.
Mr. FOWLER, I have no doubt they want all that is asked for here, but it does not seem to me in accordance with the rules that have heretofore obtained in this parliament to give a company the very extensive powers that it is proposed to give to this one.

Section agreed to.
On section 5,

This is pretty broad. It does not say that these various works shall be only in connection with the company's collieries. It lays it down broadly, and the works enumerated might be works of a general character entirely separate and apart from the object of the company.
On section 14,
Section 18 and such other provisions of the ' Companies Clauses Act ' as may be inconsistent with the provisions of the ' Companies Acts, 1862 to 1890,' of Great Britain, or of any statutes of the imperial parliament in amendment thereof, or in substitution therefor, shall not apply to the company.

This is a very remarkable clause : it involves the necessity of comparing our Companies Clauses Act with the Companies Clauses Act of Great Britain and with any Acts that may be passed in the future in amendment of that Act by the imperial parliament and of thus ascertaining whether the conditions of the one are consistent with those of the other. It is the most remarkable clause I ever observed in any Bill brought before this parliament. I think the whole Bill ought to receive more careful consideration by the government than it appears to have received.
I have done my duty in calling attention to-

it. I do not believe this Bill in the present form will be in the interest of the country or of the corporation itself. You have some amendments evidently made to its powers as granted under the Companies Act, of Great Britain. I would think tbe best way to deal with a corporation of this kind would be to let it act under its powers as originally created. It can be constituted under the Companies Act of Great Britain with powers to operate a business in this country. Then, if it requires for its undertaking in Canada any powers, such as the expropriation of land, the building of railways, <&c., this parliament might very reasonably afford such powers to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not had my attention especially directed to this Bill, and it seems to me that if this were the first departure we should hesitate before going further. I remember, however, that last year we put through a Bill somewhat on the same lines. I would like to suggest to the gentlemen responsible for this Bill the question whether they have considered that under our Companies Act provision is made for the incorporation of foreign companies with all the powers which such companies possess so far as not inconsistent with our own Act. It seems to me that might all have been done under the ordinary Companies Clauses Act without coming before parliament at all, and I quite appreciate that when it comes before parliament it should be dealt with with considerable care. Under the circumstances I would ask that the 'committee rise and report progress so that I may have an opportunity of looking into the matter further.

I would think that for the construction of a small branch of railway, the power of expropriating land, the erection of a telegraph line, &c., the company might desire some legislation here, and I would not object to giving those powers, but it does not seem to me that the Act has been drawn up on a very scientific or logical basis. It mixes up the powers conferred by this parliament with the original constitution of the company, and then in the very last clause, which we are now considering, it calls upon those who seek to ascertain the powers of the company, to study this statute, the memorandum and articles of the company, the English Companies Act and all amendments to it, the Companies Clauses Act of Canada and to find out if possible from all of these what the powers of the company are. I should think that a good lawyer labouring 8 or 10 hours a day might possibly work out the powers of the company in 10 days or a fortnight.

Say 20 hours a day.
Mr. R, L. BORDEN. I am suggesting a very diligent and skilful lawyer, but it might take longer for most of us. Under
these circumstances I would think it as well that those who are promoting the company should have a little care as to the form in which this Bill goes through parliament.

The gentleman who appeared before the Private Bills Committee stated that the members of the company reside I think, in France. They first went to London and sought incorporation, but then they found that would not serve the whole of their purpose, and they wrote to instruct this solicitor to get a charter here. We made a great many suggestions to him as to the manner in which he might proceed but of course he was in the awkward position of not being able to communicate with his clients as they resided at so great a distance. The committee dealt with the Bill in the best manner they could.

I would like some one to explain to me what that last clause means. Nobody seems to know what it means, and I do not think this parliament should pass a clause of that kind without some explanation being given. Section 14 reads :
Section 18 and any such other provisions of the Companies Clauses Act as may be inconsistent with the provisions of the ' Companies Acts, 1862 to 1890,' of Great Britain, or of any statutes of the imperial parliament in amendment thereof, or in substitution herefor, shall not apply to the company.

The meaning of that was this :	The provision which was submitted
to the committee was that no portion of the Companies' Clauses Act should apply to the promoters of the Bill, wanted their charter to be under the English Companies' Act. There was a good deal of discussion over it and it was framed in such a way as to proride that only such portions of the Canadian Companies' Clauses Act as are not inconsistent with the English Companies' Act, should apply ; so that only the English Companies' Act and the remainder of the Canadian Companies' Clauses Act, if there is any remainder, shall apply to this Bill.
It seems to me to bring in any future statutes of the imperial parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, it would.

The head office is in London and. they wanted to carry on their business from London. At least that is what was represented to the committee. It was represented that they were organized under the English Companies' Act and they did not want to be subject to two Companies' Acts. We did not think it made very much difference one way or the other.

I would call the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice to this clause. It seems to me that this parliament should not pass such loose legislation as is proposed by this Bill. Who

is going to interpret the clauses of our Act. compare them with the clauses of the English Companies' Act, 1862 to 1890, and say where they are inconsistent ? Is it going to be liable to the interpretation of the court, and is this company going to get from this parliament powers which are certainly not defined in this Bill ? It seems to me that we are going very far in the matter of private legislation and that the hon. Minister of Justice and government should take some care in seeing that Bills which are passed here in relation to private matters should he such as would be easily interpreted and not require the examination, not only of our own Acts in regard to companies hut also of the English Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) must be aware that the Minister of Justice is not responsible for private legislation. There is no principle better understood than that. I have no responsibility for drafting the private Bills that go through this House. Parliament is responsible for that, not the Minister of Justice. I am responsible for the legislation that I introduce into this House. If I were to be made personally responsible for all the private Bills that go through parliament it would be absolutely necessary for me to do nothing else.

I take a wider view of the scope of the duties of my hon. friend. I do not mean to say that he could be held responsible for all the private Bills which go before the private Bills committee, and which come before this House, but, on the other hand I say that he has the general supervision of legislation- both public and private which comes before parliament and if his attention is drawn to any such flagrant mis-use of the powers conferred upon this parliament in regard to private legislation as seems to be included in this Bill, his duty, I respectfully submit, is to see that this legislation is properly curtailed and kept within bounds.

Mr. Chairman, as the Bill is standing in my name I would like to say that I have no objection in view of what lias been said by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) and the hon. leader of the opposition (Sir. R. L. Borden) to have the Bill reviewed either by the private Bills committee or some other special committee if it is thought necessary. But, I would like to point out that the Bill relates to an existing company, a company having extensive operations both in coal mining and railways, and as I understand the purpose of the Bill it is to combine under one name and under one organization several enterprises which are really the property of the same individuals who constitute this company. I did not follow the discussion very accurately but I would not wish whoever is reviewing the Bill again to think that this is only! a question as between British legislation and

Canadian legislation. It is not something which is merely a question of law. There is a matter of business to be settled. There is an existing company which has spent a very large amount of money in active coal mining operations and in the building of a short line of railway and the members of the company, having entered upon kindred enterprises in the vicinity, now desire to have all these enterprises amalgamated under one name and have a single set of powers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Minister of Justice moves that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
What is the suggestion of the hon. Minister of Justice in reference to that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would like to have a chance to look over this Bill not having seen it except hurriedly at the present time, and especially in respect to the amendments.
I am. perhaps, somewhat slow of comprehension, and I like an opportunity of considering anything before expressing my opinion about it. I would like to have these amendments before me so that I may consider them. I do not agree with the view which apparently obtains in this House that a company ought to be granted for a special purpose only. I. think that incorporation ought to be granted to companies for any purpose for which parliament wishes to confer powers on them. I fail to understand the reason of the rule which has apparently been adopted up to the present time, but I would not endeavoui; to press my personal view as against the view of the House upon that point.
Is it understood that when the committee rises and reports progress, the hon. Minister of Justice shall take the responsibility of reviewing the Bill ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Motion agreed to, and progress reported.

House in Committee on Bill (No. 79) to incorporate the Thompson River Improvement Company.-Mr. Morrison.
On section 12,
Was this section expunged in the Private Bills Committee V
Yes.
W'hy ?

Very strong objection was taken by some members of the committee who are familiar with the business of this company, and who are engaged in similar business themselves. We thought the whole matter was covered by section 11, and so clause 12 was stricken out and the tolls

would laave to be submitted to the Governor in Council wbere all parties could be heard.
Does not the Columbia River Improvement Bill of last year, contain a clause similar to this clause 12 ?
Yes. but we thought that section 11 was all that was required.
The result is that before tolls are charged by this company they have to go to the Governor in Council and get them approved.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would ' my hon. friend point out where we get jurisdiction at all in this matter ?

That question was debated at considerable length in the committee. My own view was that the jurisdiction was entirely in the province, but the majority thought that as we had been conferring similar powers on other companies we should do so for this company.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am disposed to consider that it is not within our power to pass this Bill.
That is the view I held at first.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot see anything in the Bill which shows that it has reference exclusively to navigable waters. It is not because we passed the Columbia River Bill yast year that we should pursue the same course this year. When we were passing that Bill last year, it occurred [DOT] to me that we were going beyond our powers.
This river is navigable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: How far is it navigable ?
For nearly two hundred miles.
We held that it was a navigable river, and that it was necessary to come to this parliament. The only question in my mind was as to whether they should not go to the provincial parliament as well.
Was any information given to the committee as to whether this river is navigable at the point mentioned in the Bill ?

This river is navigable for nearly two hundred miles of its length. The Kamloops lake is navigable; the town of Kamloops is situated at the confluence of the North Thompson and South Thompson rivers. And the North Thompson is navigable for quite two hundred miles. It was necessary to come here and get these rights, and I may say that an application has also been made to the provincial legislature. 1

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is a clause here which gives power to blast rocks and remove shoals and other impediments. It is quite clear that it has reference to some part of the river that is not navigable.

In order to place the position of the committee before the House, I wish to say that the majority of the committee were firmly of the opinion that this parliament did not have exclusive jurisdiction. The Bill deals with tributaries and with branches which are not navigable. We felt that we did not have the right to give power to attach the booms to the shore ; and that that was entirely within the jurisdiction of the province.
I know of my own knowledge that the river is navigable for at least two hundred miles, and that steamers ply on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It turns on a question of fact.

That is a matter of fact. Steamers in which I am interested have ascended the river for one hundred and fifty miles from where It joins the South Thompson up towards its source, and therefore it was necessary'to come to this parliament. An application has been made to the provincial parliament as well.
Very likely it is a case in which the complete carrying out of the undertaking would involve legislation from this parliament, as well as from the provincial parliament.
I think so.

We discussed that point, and I was of that opinion ; but it seemed to me that if the parliament of Canada had any jurisdiction at all in consequence of this being a work which would obstruct navigation, that then the attaching of booms to the shores would be a purely incidental matter and this parliament would have jurisdiction.
I would doubt that a little.

My hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) can take his Bill and the risk with it.

speechtext:
Mr. LEFURGEY-by Mr. Hackett-asked:
1.	On what principle are bounties paid to fishermen in the maritime provinces.?
