For copies of all correspondence between the government, and any person, or persons, in reference to the granting of pensions to those of the Canadian South African contingents who were wounded or suffered any disability in such service.

He said : Mr. Speaker,*1 wish, if possible to find out whether or not the government has settle^ on any policy in reference to these men. Those who have suffered disability are in receipt of small pensions from the British government; but that pension is altogether inadequate for their maintenance, particularly in the cases of serious disability. I do not wish in any sense to detract from the claim set up on behalf of any man who participated in that war when the whole world was jealously watching every movement of England and wishing the success of her enemy's arms. The men,who went out from Canada to defend the empire on that occasion did a great deal for the furtherance of Canadian interests, not only in England, but in other countries. The benefit which Canada derived and is still deriving from the efforts of those men, voluntarily undertaken, and the personal sacrifices they made, should call forth the gratitude of the Canadian people, especially to those who suffered at the hands of the enemy. In my own county there is a young man who joined the ranks and went to South Africa, and became totally disabled by losing the sight of both eyes. I need not inform this House that I refer to Trooper Mulloy. Wherever the English language is spoken, the name of Trooper Mulloy is known ; and if it is not the general policy of this government to do something for every one who suffered a disability, there certainly should be some definite policy with regard to him. He receives at the hands of the British government 65 cents per day. He is a young man of more than ordinary ability. He is a young man who previous to his disability, was inspired with an ambition to make his mark in the world, and he is now going to college under great difficulties, having to employ assistance in his work in order to place himself in a position to make some sort of livelihood. I have known his family for many years, and they are a family whom every man in this House would respect if he knew them. Out of respect for the family I do not wish to refer to their financial position. I can say this, however, that there was a time when they were very well off, being well-to-do farmers. But circumstances have changed since then, and they are not as well off to-day as they were some years ago ; and, Sir, the responsibility will to some extent rest on this young man of maintaining his aged mother, with whom I think it is his intention to make his home while she remains here. If the government intend to do anything in this matter, it is high time for them to make some announcement of their policy. This young man, I believe, has drawn some $2,000 all told from the patriotic fund, which was subscribed by private citizens some years ago ; but that is not a fund on which the country has a right to throw any individual. The

country's gratitude ought to extend to these individuals. I do not suppose there is a country in the world outside of Canada which would leave these persons in the position in which they are to-day. I do not say that we ought to copy to' the fullest extent the pension policy of the United Stiltes ; but there is this to be said, that no American citizen suffers from having fought for his country's rights without receiving full recognition, no matter where he may live ; and if we are ever to have a full and free Canadian sentiment in this country, we shall have to recognize the claims of men who are willing to step into the ranks and defend the country's interests when trouble is at her doors. It is all very well to discuss the question as to whether or not we have a right to have anything to do with the imperial wars, and all that sort of thing ; but we cannot expect our citizens to stand on the threshold of their country's troubles and discuss who is right and who is wrong before they fight in her interest. If these young men had done that, Canada would never have benefited from their efforts in South Africa. I think this question ought to be put at rest by some announcement from the government to day in reference to what they intend to do. I do not wish to prolong this discussion or to say anything that would offend the sensibilities of any man, but I wish to urge on the government the necessity and advisability of doing something in this instance.

Last year my hon. friend spoke to me several times during the session privately with reference to this matter, and I informed him that I intended to bring it up some time during the session. At my request he postponed bringing the matter before the House, as I was in hopes that I might be able to give him some answer. I told him on the occasions when we talked it over that the pension list was being prepared by the imperial government, and I thought it wise to postpone consideration of any particular case until we could consider the whole. Unfortunately the matter was brought up by my hon. friend when I was not present, but that was no fault of his. He had postponed it at my request until nearly the end of the session, when I was called away and he had to bring it up in my absence. 1 have read the debate which then took place and I have had the pleasure of hearing what my hon. friend has said to-day, in a great part of which I entirely agree. There can be no question as to the nobility of the conduct of those representatives of Canada who served in South Africa. There are some reasons, which may be known to some hon. members of this House, which are known to my hon. friend at any rate, with reference to Trooper Molloy which should appeal specially and personally to me. However, in considering matters of this kind, we
must proceed on general lines. It is not, I think, desirable that we should deal with individual cases except perhaps in very rare instances. The work of classifying and determining the merits of the applications which have been made for pensions by Canadians who served in South Africa has not even yet been completed. I should have said that the men who enlisted in Canada for service in South Africa were perfectly well aware that they entered into a contract with the imperial government to accept from it the same treatment as imperial soldiers received. The work of determining the list has been going on for two years. There are something like ninety provisional or temporary pensioners, that is ^pensioners receiving pensions for a limited period of time. There are something like twenty getting permanent pensions. The list is not concluded, but the result will probably be that there will be about thirty permanent pensioners and something over a hundred pensioners for a term, which may or may not be renewed according to the deserts of the special or individual case.
What authority is giving the pensions ?
The imperial government.
Is the Canadian government ?
No, that is not the arrangement.
I do not understand the reference to the lists not being completed.

The question seems to resolve' itself into this. We have a pension list in this country. We are paying pensioners who served in the Fenian raid. We are paying pensioners who served in the Northwest rebellion. Surely they deserve as much consideration as the men who served in South Africa. Surely the men who defended the integrity of the soil of Canada against the invader and put down rebellion within this country are entitled to as much consideration as those who served the army in South Africa. The logical result then is that we should apply the pension rate in Canada, but not more, to the men who are pensioned upon the British government and who served in South Africa.
There were some who received special treatment.
None so far as I know.
Oh, yes.

I was not aware of that. However, the point I am going to make is this. In whatever we do we must proceed upon the same lines as we have proceeded upon in the past and apply

the same rules, and I am quite willing to do that. If it should turn out that the pensions which the men who have served in South Africa are receiving is below the Canadian pension, I should say we should do exactly agi we did in the case of the pay.. The House will remember that the parliament of Canada supplemented to the Canadians who served in South Africa the difference between the imperial rate of pay and the Canadian, and upon the same principle,
I would be disposed to make up to the South African pensioners any difference that there may be( between the rate of the imperial pension and the rate of the Canadian pension.
What is the difference ?

I am not able to say but I do not think there is any very material difference. I have made some inquiry, and I believe that the Canadiau pension would not be materially if at all higher than the pension which Molloy is now receiving, but there would be a difference in some cases, and generally speaking I believe the Canadian rate of pension is slightly higher than the imperial rate. That is as much as I am able to say to-day, but as soon as the list is completed, I will look carefully into the case. The papers which my hon. friend has asked for will be brought down, and I hope, before the end of the session, to be able to make some explicit statement as to what will be done.
Motion agreed to.

CHASE CASGRAIN (Montmorency) moved for :
Copies of all deeds, papers, documents, correspondence, &c., now existing in any department, and filed since the 15th of September, 1903, in relation to the contract executed in the course of last session, for the establishment of a line of steamers between Canada and France ; and to the subsidy payable for the said purpose ; or to any matter-or subject connected with the said contract and the said subsidy.	[DOT]
He said : It will be remembered that when this question was brought up last year everybody was agreed that if a first-rate line were established between some port in France and a port in Canada, the commerce of this country would greatly benefit, and when the resolutions were brought down, granting $133,000 a year for ten years towards the establishment of this new line, it passed without a dissenting voice.
Now, it will also be remembered that, when the matter was brought up last year, it was stated by the right hon. leader of the. House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that negotiations were being carried on with one M.

Colombier of Bordeaux. And, when it was asked what references had been asked for in relation to M. Colombier's standing and financial ability, a telegram was produced from the British consul at Bordeaux saying that the Hoqse of Colombier was a respectable house, not of very large means, but quite able to grapple with the proposition that was at its door. It was suggested at , the time, and my hon. friends on the other side were warned from this side, and warned very pointedly, that probably M. Colombier was not the prime mover in this scheme but that he was personne inter-posee and for the purpose of giving the contract to one Mr. Carbonneau. Now, Mr. Carbonneau had not enjoyed, up to that time; a very savoury reputation in Canada ; and I must say, that reputation has not been enhanced by his actions since in Canada or France. But hon. gentlemen opposite were yery set, and declared that they did not know Mr. Carbonneau officially, but that all negotiations were being carried on with M. Colombier and not with Mr. Carbonneau. On several occasions my hon. friends on the other side were told by gentlemen on this side of the House that Mr. Carbonneau was really the person interested and that M. Colombier was only acting for Mr. Carbonneau. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. PrSfontaine) who I regret not to see in his place to-day gave us assurance in these words, which I quote from ' Hansard ' :
On this occasion the government is taking every precaution to achieve success.
For, it had been pointed out that this was 'a third or fourth attempt to establish a line of steamers between France and Canada and it would be too bad if, on this fourth occasion, the scheme fell through.
It was all the more important to establish a line of steamers between Canada and France because it was almost, if not quite, impossible to derive benefit from the Franco-Canadian treaty which had been entered into some time before, unless we had steamers plying between France and Canada. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine 'and Fisheries (Mr. Prefontaine) who came before the House with considerable data, and who seems to be the spon&or of this line and to have many friends amongst those who were connected with the enterprise, even went so far as to tell us that four ships were then under contract to be built and delivered by the 1st of April. 1904. I do not know where he got his information. It was precise information and, from it, it seemed that everything was ready so that these gentlemen not only could get the $133,000 that the contract gave them, but that this line of steamers would certainly be established for this season of navigation. Now, we find from answers which I had the honour of putting to the government, that very soon after

the end of last session if not while the session was still in progress, the contract given to M. Colombier was transferred to Mr. Carbonneau whom the government did not know officially. They had been warned, at that time, as I have said, that Mr. Carbonneau seemed to be the principal agent and principal factor in this scheme-the head pusher as my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) suggests. The government ignored Mr. Car-bonneau ; they did not know him officially. Yet, strange to say, almost immediately after the contract had been entered into between M. Colombier and the government that contract was transferred to Mr. Carbonneau. And what: do we find further ? We find that Mr. Carbonneau afterwards transferred the contract to some company by the name of Le Transport Canadien, Limited. Now, the line has not been established. It is true that two steamers have made two trips from France to Canada. The first steamers sailed from some port in France-Bordeaux I believe, calling at St. Pierre et Miquelon Islands and coming as far as Halifax. Of that trip. we have very little information. Another trip was made by a steamer called the ' Malou ' which arrived out the other day from the port of Bordeaux at Montreal. Concerning this, we have more information. The vessel seems to have carried quite a number of passengers, but, if the information in the newspapers is correct, the steamer was not at all fitted for the service. In fact, the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in answer to questions that I put, said that it was not admitted by the government that by causing the sailing of this steamer to a Canadian port M. Colombier had fulfilled any of the obligations he had entered into under the law passed last session. Now, it seems, the government are in negotiations with the linn of Armstrong. How they have got into the game-because it seem^ like a game-I do not understand. I do not know whether Mr. Carbonneau, after transferring his contract to the Transport Canadien has transferred it to the Armstrongs. If current rumour is true, Mr. Carbonneau has transferred the contract a second time to the firm of Armstrong which is now in negotiation with the government. All this will appear in the papers which I ask to have brought down. I would ask the government also to bring down the contract which was entered into last year. It is not mentioned in my motion, but, if necessary, I would ask leave to amend my motion to cover that.
I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Casgrain) will find that the contract has been laid on the table.

It was laid on the table, but I cannot find any trace of it in any of
the departments of the House. I have searched all the offices of the House, but cannot find it anywhere. I applied to the clerk without success. Through some mistake, it seems to have been taken away and it is not available. Under these circumstances. if necessary,' I will ask to amend my motion so that a copy of the contract may be produced with the other papers.
At all events I think it is in order for us to call the attention of the government to the fact that what we said last year is true, that the prime mover in this scheme was Mr. Carbonneau. and the government should have taken special precautions to see that he had nothing to do with the contract, especially that he should not be the principal person contracted with under the name of M. Colombier. Mr. Carbonneau is well known in this country. His reputation was made a good while before this contract was negotiated for. He was connected-as was pointed out-with an enterprise in Montreal which fell to the ground and which was one of the causes w-hy La Banque du Peuple had to go out of existence. And his reputation was not bettered by anything he did on the other side, either in England or in France. And I know that before the end of the session and before the Bill actually passed, certain papers were handed over to my right hon. friend the leader of the House in which the past career of Mr. Carbonneau was exposed. Now, Mr. Carbonneau to-day is practically a fugitive from justice. He cannot go to France. He cannot set foot in England. He cannot come to Montreal, because a dozen capiases have been issued against him, and he will be arrested as soon as he appears in that city. He cannot go to the Yukon. So, here is a man who was pointed out to the government by hon. gentlemen on this side as the principal one with whom they were contracting. It was known to everybody except the government that Mr. Carbonneau was at the bottom of this scheme. All the ministers were blind to the fact, but almost everybody else in the House knew that Mr. Carbonneau was really the man ; and the evidence to prove that we were right in this assumption is that when the contract was passed between M. Colombier and the government, it was immediately transferred to Mr. Carbonneau. I hope the papers will be brought down as soon as possible, because, of course, this is a matter that must be fully ventilated in this House. I would ask permission to amend my motion by ad'ding :
And also a copy of the contract executed between the government and M. Colombier.
My hon. friend, 1 think, will find that contract in the hands of some of the hon. gentlemen on the other side, but, of course, I have no objection in the world to the motion or the amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As has already been stated by the hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright), there is no objection to these papers being brought down and they will be brought down immediately. My hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) has thought it advisable to pass some strictures on the government because it was reported last year that Mr. Carbonneau was behind this project. This report was true ; he was behind the project, but the government had nothing to do with him. It insisted on having all negotiations with M. Colombier, who belongs to a very respectable house. The report, as I say, was quite true, as I understand, but we had no-official knowledge of the fact in the department. It has been reported, and I believe it is beyond doubt, that almost immediately after the contract was signed it was transferred by Mr. Carbonneau to M. Colombier, who transferred it to a company called the Transport Canadien. The government would not recognize this assignment. The criticism of my hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) would certainly be entitled to great weight if it were shown that the government had, had anything to do with Mr. Carbonneau and had been willing to recognize or to accept the assignments said to have been made by M. Colombier to Mr. Carbonneau and by Mr. Carbonneau to the Transport Canadien. But the government did nothing of the kind ; the government held Mr. Colombier strictly to his contract, and I am sorry to say that we have been once more disappointed, and that M. Colombier has not been able to carry out his contract. The merely colourable attempt which has been made to implement the contract is one which cannot be entertained. So far as I know, only one ship has been sent out by M. Colombier, that is the ship to which my hon. friend has just referred, the ' Malou.' The ' Malou ' left St. Malo on the 2nd of May. It touched at St. Pierre and Miquelon, where it lef|t a large number of fishermen of the class who always come there especially to fish on the Crand Banks, then proceeded to Halifax, and I believe also went to Montreal and landed some immigrants.
And to New York also.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
And to New York, so it is impossible to ackowledge that as accomplishing the agreement, and M. Colombier has been notified that his contract will be cancelled and all assignments made toy him -will not be recognized. The government has had some inquiries and some negotiations also with the firm of Armstrong & Whitworth, the large shipbuilding firm. These negotiations with the great firm of Armstrong & Company have not yet been completed, and if the firm of Armstrong, Whitworth & Company are willing to enter into a contract w'ith us, I think we could do nothing better than enter into a contract with such a respectable firm as this. We 1 Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
woul3 then have what we have so long wished to have, a service to France, which has not yet been obtained.
The government do not seem to have been very much more successful with this enterprise than with the fast Atlantic service, at least up to the present time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No ; it has baffled the efforts of many governments.

It seems remarkable that we should have a statement last session from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that four ships would be completed by the spring of this year. It now appears that no ship has been even commenced, much less completed. When a responsible minister of the Crown makes a statement of that kind to parliament, and it has been so absolutely lacking in fulfilment, one would think my right hon. friend would think it worthy of some explanation when responding to the motion of my hon. friend (Mr, Casgrain). On what basis, on what authority, from what information, did the Minister of Marine and Fisheries make so extraordinary a statement to the House last year ? It seems to me to be absolutely unheard of that such a statement should have been made in this House when it seems to have been absolutely lacking in any foundation whatever. One could hardly suppose the Minister of Marine and Fisheries would toe so reckless in his statements to the House as to pass a remark of that kind without some authority or foundation for it, and yet we are not informed of any reason that he had for giving to the House so important a piece of information.
The right hon. gentleman says that the government did not know Mr. Carbonneau. although he believes the contract was assigned to him almost immediately after being entered into. Can it be true that if the government did not know Carbonneau officially, it really knew him practiciflly, and was weld aware that at the time that the contract was being made for his benefit, and with the intention that it should he assigned to him 7 That has been the current rumour, and if I am not mistaken it has been repeated more than once in the press. Under these circumstances, it hardly seems a justification to say that the government did not officially know Carbonneau if, as a matter of fact, a member of the government who has made important statements to the House on the subject did know and negotiate with Carbonneau and was aware that the contract was proposed to be assigned to him. However, when the papers are brought down we will have further information, and there will be further opportunity of discussion. In the absence of the documents to which my hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) has referred, we have little information, and I should think that at some time

before the end of the session we might at least be favoured by the government with some information of the extraordinary statements to which attention has been' called. Every one in this country would naturally suppose that by this time we would have had four steamships engaged in a profitable and advantageous trade between France and this country. Instead of that we have nothing accomplished and are exactly where we were last year, the government still continuing negotiations. The only difference between this and the fast Atlantic service seems to be that while the government is continuing negotiations in this case, it has absolutely abandoned negotiations in the other case. I am depending for that statement on the authority of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who, I think, gives the House to understand that. How long will it be before the two enterprises are exactly on the same footing, namely, that nothing shall have been accomplished and no negotiations shall be in progress ? Perhaps we might have a prophesy on that from the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright), who, from his experience, will be well able to inform the House just how long it will be before the government will abandon negotiations, having accomplished nothing in regard to the service between France and this country.
Perhaps my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce would not like to hazard a prophecy, but if any one in the House could give us any information upon that subject I would suppose that he should be called upon to do it. It is a pity the service has not been proceeded with. I assume that the government have taken it up on good grounds. I do not recollect all the data which was placed before the House last year but I recollect that I was impressed with the idea that service would be beneficial to this country and would build up some trade. It is therefore to be regretted that nothing has been accomplished and I trust that before the end of the session we shall have some further information about, the negotiations, because, in matters of this kind, we have become so accustomed to the methods of the government that we feel that even when negotiations are going on we have not reached that hopeless condition in which the fast Atlantic service finds itself to-day.
The late government were negotiating for a long time for a fast Atlantic service.
And they would have accomplished something if this government had not interfered.

On section 1,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This Bill is introduced for the purpose of removing a doubt suggested by the terms of section 5 of the Act as it now stands. That section provides for the incorporation by letters-patent of companies for any of the purposes or objects to which the legislative authority of parliament extends, and it then proceeds to say :
Except the construction and working of railways, or of telegraph or of telephone lines, or the business of banking and the issue of paper money, or the business of insurance, or the business of a loan company.
It is conceivable that this exception might be construed to cover the class of companies mentioned in the proposed subsection, although really it was not intended to do that. I quite agree that possibly a doubt may exist, and that it is desirable to remove that doubt, but I do not think my hon. friend has gone about it in the proper way. If he would pardon me, I would suggest that

that doubt should be removed by enacting provisions to the following effect :
The expression, * the construction and working of railways, or of telegraph, or of telephone lines,' in section 5 of the Companies Act, 1902, does not include the acting as a contractor in railway or telegraph, or telephone construction ; and nothing in the said Act shall he deemed or taken to prevent or to have prevented the granting thereunder of a charter by letters patent constituting a company for the purpose of acting as such contractor.
2. The expression, * construction and working of railways ' in section 3 of the Companies Act, chapter 117 of the revised statutes, does not include acting as a contractor in railway construction, and nothing in the said Act shall bo deemed or taken to prevent or to have prevented the granting thereunder of a charter by letters patent, constituting a company for the purpose of acting as said contractor.
I move that these clauses be substituted for the first clause of this Bill.
What does section 5 provide now ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The evident intention of parliament was to reserve for parliament the incorporation of companies having for their object the construction and the working of railways, or telegraphs, or telephone lines, and also companies incorporated to carry on the business of banking and the issue of paper money, and the business of insurance or the business of a loan company. The amendment would declare that a company could be formed for the purposes of contracting for the construction of a railway or of a telephone or .telephone line. Instead of adopting the amendment suggested by the member for Essex (Mr. Cowan) I put in an interpretation clause so as to make it quite apparent that all we want to do is to declare that a company may be formed by letters patent, not to operate a railway or a telegraph, or a telephone line, but merely for the purpose of doing the contractors' work in building it.
A person requiring anything further than that would have to get a special Act of Parliament ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

House resumed adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Mr. Lennox for the second reading of Bill (No. 73) to amend the Railway Act.
I have already spoken on this matter. I presume the Minister of Justice will give his views.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Since this Bill was under consideration before, I have looked into it further, and I cannot see that there is any difference between it and the Bill introduced last session by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). This Bill is somewhat different in form., but in substance it is the same, and it is subject to the objection I then urged, which was that the Bill was unconstitutional and beyond the powers of this parliament to pass. The argument in support of the constitutional propriety of the legislation, so far as it depends on the claim of jurisdiction, appears to be based on subsections 10 and 11 of section 92 of the British North America Act. I cannot see how it is possible for us, under any proper construction of that Act, to claim that we have jurisdiction with respect to railways beyond those matters affecting their construction, operation and management. I would like to draw my hon. friend's attention to a case which I do not think he mentioned, that is, the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway vs. the County and Township of York, where, at page 70 of the 25th volume of the Appeal Reports of Ontario, Chief Justice Burton says :
The railway in question is one of the subjects placed under the exclusive jurisdiction, of the parliament of the Dominion, and it follows that in all matters affecting its construe-tioin,. Operation {and management, including the expropriation of the lands required- everything, in fact, necessary to its full and efficient working-the legislation of the Dominion is of paramount authority, even though it interferes with property and civil rights, and trenches on matters assigned to the provincial legislature by section 92 of the British North America Act.
Again, the question was up for consideration in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway vs. Notre Dame de Bonsecours, which my hon. friend will find in the Privy Council reports for 1889, page 367. There it was held that railway legislation, strictly so called, is the measure of parliament's jurisdiction. So far as complete provision for these purposes requires it, parliament has power also to deal with matters assigned to the local legislatures, but we cannot go any further than that. Under this Bill my hon. friend has in comtemplation a distinct in-

terference with a civil contract made in a province between an employer and an employee, and I think that the only way he could attempt for a moment to justify our interfering in a matter of that kind would be to deal with it as a matter affecting insurance or the regulation of trade and commerce. In the case of the Citizens' Insurance Company vs. Parsons, Appeal Cases, page 112, their Lordships say :
Regulation of trade and commerce includes political arrangements in regard to trade, requiring the sanction of parliament, regulation of trade in matters of interprovincial concern, and may, perhaps, include general regulation of trade affecting the whole Dominion, hut it does not comprehend the power to regulate by legislation the contracts of a particular business or trade (such as the business of fire insurance) in a single province.
Then Sir Horace Davey, in regard to the Dominion License Act, arguing, said :
Regulation of trade and commerce means general regulations as applicable to trade generally, of what may he called, for want of a better word, a political character, that is, for regulating trade and commerce between the Dominion and foreign countries, or, for instance, for regulating the trade between the provinces themselves. But it does not include minute regulations affecting the terms and conditions on which persons carrying on particular trades are allowed to do so in particular localities.
It seems to me the passage of this Bill would be a distinct interference with the rights of the provinces with respect to the relations between the employer and the employee, a distinct interference with what I would call a civil contract within a province. On that ground I object to this legislation, as I did to the legislation introduced last session by my hon. friend from [DOT]South Wellington.

I recognize iu this Bill language very similar, and propositions very similar, to those contained in Bills with a similar object introduced by me last session and the session before last. This Bill is, perhaps, more radical thaii the Bills I introduced, as it absolutely takes away the right of the employee to contract himself out of liability. The Bill which I introduced on two former occasions left the right of contract but allowed the reasonableness of the contract to be decided by a court or a judge. Now, the great difficulty in the case is this :	That no plaintiff so
far, has had financial resources sufficient to get a decision from an Appellate Court. There are two judgments now upholding the rights of the railway companies but

they are only the judgments of trial judges. It may be that the case would be otherwise decided by the Supreme Court or the Privy Council; but it is not very likely that we shall have a plaintiff who is able to go that length. I would ask the Minister of Justice whether, having regard to the fact that there are some 25,000 or 30,000 railway employees, he would or would not be disposed to state the facts and submit a case to the Supreme Court for their opinion as to the constitutionality of the Act now before us. If the Ontario Act does apply, that is an end of it, and if it does not, then some legislation such as this, I think, might well be passed by this parliament.

I was not present when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) made his remarks with respect to this Bill, but I understand that his contention is that this parliament has no jurisdiction in the matter. The present state of affairs was created by the legislation passed by this parliament in 1874 and 1878.
' That is the way I understand it. That legislation gives the Grand Trunk Railway the authority to organize this insurance company and to make just such contracts as are being made. That being the case, surely this parliament has the right to regulate the legislation it passed on those occasions. It seems to me that the merits of the case are very strong so far as the employees are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not touch the merits.

I understand perfectly that the Minister of Justice did not argue the merits of the case, but has simply given his view of the law. But the merits are so strong that, where there is a reasonable doubt-rand I think there must be a reasonable doubt in the minister's mind-it seems to me he ought to allow this legislation to go through and then let the railway companies fight it out in the courts if parliament has not the jurisdiction. The number of railway employees in the country is very large and is rapidly increasing, and, if the Grand Trunk Pacific is carried through there will be many more. It seems to me that some relief is absolutely necessary. Look at the circumstances. A man goes into this employment which, as was stated by the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) is a hazardous one. His wages, while, perhaps, a reasonable return for his labour, are not large. He makes a contract with his employer-must do it in order to be employed-not to seek damages in case he is injured, no matter how much fault there may be on the part of the employer. And if he is killed his family is precluded from seeking compensation for loss of the bread-winner. This is an undesirable state of affairs and one which parliament should Mr. GUTHRIE.	.
seen to remedy. This is the only place these people can come to for redress of their grievances, and this Bill is calculated to give that redress. It seems strange that this parliament, which controls the Intercolonial should, not, in this case at least arrange to have this obnoxious clause abolished, so that, when employees of the Intercolonial, if injured through the negligence of their fellow employees shall receive compensation for such injuries. The authorities are very clear. There is a case reported in 30, Supreme Court of Canada in which the chief justice gives his opinion that this contract can be enforced so far as the railway is concerned. We have here the judgment of the highest court of the land upholding this sort of contract. Therefore, the only way to get clear of it is by some such legislation as that proposed in this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is that Grenier vs. the Queen ?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is a case I argued myself.
Yes, the case was argued by the Minister of Justice himself. It seems to me there can be no question as to what the judgment of the court was.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The judgment was all right.
It seems to me the case was exactly in point.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, but they held the contract good-

That is what I say.
Mr. FITZPATRICK-under the civil law of the province.
Do I understand the minister to say that we should interfere with provincial rights in passing such legislation as this ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
This is a Dominion railway. Surely, we have the right to pass legislation incidental to the working of the road.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: ' Construction, maintenance and operation.'
This comes under the head of operation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would add a word to what I have already said. There is something in the suggestion of my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) as to the propriety of having the question decided. I have no doubt as to the soundness of the position I have assumed. But I have asked my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) who promotes the Bill to have it referred to the

committee. We can discuss it there. My view is that we might gain the object sought by making an amendment to section 242 of the Railway Act. And, as I have already expressed doubt as to the constitutionality of a part of subsection 3 of section 242, I do not know but that it would be wise to make an amendment that would meet his views, and then perhaps we might have a reference to the Supreme Court to have the matter decided. I do not pretend, while I have my own opinions on this subject, that I know everything that is to be known about it, and I quite appreciate the importance of coming to the assistance of these people who are connected with the operation of railways. At the same time I realize the importance on the other hand, of leaving all matters respecting contract within the provinces to the laws of the province, and in the case of Grenier vs. the Queen the Supreme Court decided formally that a contract entered into by the husband of the woman who was the plaintif in the case was binding on both parties. The question was raised and discussed. I was present and expressed that opinion and my opinion was sustained by tire court.
That is the difficulty. If the contract was not binding it would not be necessary to have legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I said that the contract is good under our civil code. This would operate with extreme hardship against the employees of railways in our province where we have no such doctrine as the law of contributory negligence and common employment. These I understand apply to the English provinces. In our province notwithstanding an accident might be caused by the negligence of a fellow-servant there is compensation but in the other provinces-
I think in all the provinces that is abrogated by statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am speaking more of the common law. In Ontario for
instance, you have the Workmen's Compensation Act. I am willing to have the matter referred to the Railway Committee where we will discuss and where I will suggest an amendment which would meet what my hon. friend has in view and in all probability- of course I cannot now speak with authority, as I have not consulted the other members of the government-we could have the matter referred to the Supreme Court for judical determination. That would be my own opinion.
As I understand it the Minister of Justice purposes referring this to the Committee of the Whole House.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, I would suggest that the matter go to the Railway Com-150$
mittee, where we may have a fuller discussion than here, and then I will myself suggest an amendment which I think will go as far as my hon. friend intends, and possibly it might be determined that the government might have the matter referred to the Supreme Court.

I understand the Minister of Justice to say that in his opinion the Bill introduced by my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) is not a constitutional Bill. Some years ago when this very legislation was brought up in the province of Ontario, after soliciting information from the Grand Trunk Railway Company-that I thinli being the only company at that time which had a Provident Insurance Society under the Act of 1874-after receiving information they concluded that the majority of the employees of the Grand Trunk were not in favour of being excluded from the benefits of the Compensation for Injuries Act of the province of Ontario, but after getting that information they placed on the statute-book an amendment to the Compensation for Injuries Act to the effect that all employees connected with the insurance society in the Grand Trunk were excluded from the provisions of the Compensation for Injuries Act and therefore it was only those who were not connected with it in any way at all who come under that Act in Ontario. What I want to know is if this Act is an extension of the redress for the railway employees of the Grand Trunk Company who are connected with the Provident Insurance Society, would they by reason of assigning away their rights or contracting themselves out of any benefit or redress which they have other than simply the usual compensation of the Provident Insurance Society.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That was the only redress.

That is a most extraordinary position. Here is a provincial government exercising control over Dominion railways. The railways for which they have apparently legislated are railways partially within one province and partially within another and therefore they hold when you go to the government of the province of Ontario that that province has no jurisdiction over these railways. The Minister of Justice shakes his head; I take it for granted they must have control according to his opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: With respect to those contracts which arise within the limits of the province.

In so far as they affect the employees Provident Insurance Society but not otherwise. I do not see how the employees who feel that this is a great hardship are going to get their grievances re-

dressed unless this parliament takes hold of the matter and places legislation on the statute-hook, legislation that will relieve them. I cannot see any other way.

I understood the Minister of Justice to say that he would move an amendment to section 242, subsection 3. I endeavoured to make it clear when moving the second reading of the Bill that I merely wanted to accomplish my purpose and would be very glad to have the assistance of the government. Why should not the Minister of Justice let the matter stand over and introduce his amendment so as to have it come up before the Committee of the Whole House at a subsequent time ? Why should we not consider it as we did the Railway Act of last session ? We did not have to go to the Railway Committee with that, and it seems to me it is a great advantage to discuss it in the whole House.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I prefer to have the matter go before the Railway Committee. There can be no loss by having it discussed very fully there. No detriment can come to my hon. friend or his Bill by having it discussed in that committee with the understanding that so far as the government is concerned we will see that the Bill is reported back to the House. Of course in so far as the reference to the Supreme Court is concerned, I can only express now my personal preference, I would prefer to recommend to the government that we should have a reference to the court, but of course I cannot commit the government now.

So far as the constitutional question is concerned, there will not be much advantage in sending the Bill to the Railway Committee, but there are other questions that affect the merits of the Bill, and to these I presume the minister refers. I have not given the constitutional questions any consideration. Has the minister any opinion as to whether it is within the power of parliament ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I have not recently given the matter careful consideration either, because I presume, in view of the decision in Grenier vs The Queen that I was committed to the view I expressed then and I have not departed from it. I think that view was upheld by the court.

I think we all agree that in the absence of legislation from the parliament of Canada the question of liability must be determined by the law of the provinces. But that is not an end of the question submitted by my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox). The question still remains whether or not this subject is so directly connected with a matter over which we have jurisdiction that this parliament can in thatJ

*
respect interfere with the law of the provinces. Of course the Minister of Justice is quite as familiar as I am, or more familiar than I am, with the extent to which the doctrine of incidental jurisdiction, if I may so express it, has been carried by the courts.
It occurred to me while the discussion was going on that it might be possible for this parliament, for example, in a Bill incorporating a railway company, or in a Bill dealing generally with railway companies, to make provision requiring notice of action. Legislation of that kind is of very frequent occurrence on the statute-book of Canada, and probably in some cases which are not very far from the matter which we are now discussing. Well, if you concede that that would be possible, you are not really very far away from what my hon. friend from Simcoe is urging. He is urging just the converse of 'that, namely', that employees engaged by that company for the operation of the road may not by contract with the company deprive themselves of certain rights in connection with injuries which they may sustain while engaged in that work. I have no strong opinion on the subject, because I have non considered it, but I think the proposition would be quite arguable, and I would be inclined to think that the course suggested by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, namely, to have the whole of this question, in connection with some other question mentioned by him, referred to the Supreme Court, would perhaps be the best course to adopt.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps I am trespassing upon the rules of the House, but I would like my hon. friend to understand my reason for, at the present time at all events, agreeing with the course proposed to be taken. A careful reading of the Grand Trunk Act does suggest a doubt on the question. Incidentally a doubt has been raised in respect to the question of jurisdiction, and in view of that doubt I would be quite satisfied to recommend to the government a reference of this question to the Supreme Court.
Do I understand my hon. friend the Minister of Justice to move that the reference of this Bill be to the Railway Committee '! I recognize that there is no use of dividing the House on the question.
The motion at present is for the Second reading only. The other motion cannot be made until the motion for the second reading is disposed of.
Do I understand the hon. minister to move that this order be discharged and that the Bill be referred to the Railway Committee ?
The proper course is to move the second reading, and then some one may move to refer the Bill to the Railway Committee.

I do not wish to be understood as agreeing to the propositions which were advanced by the lion. Minister of Justice, great deference as I certainly have for his opinion. The cases that I referred to in the argument in chief my hon. friend has not seen tit to deal with. I have referred to the cases to sustain my argument. I have endeavoured to make it clear, and I think I have from the authorities I have cited made it reasonably clear that what we can do is to restore this matter to the position in which it was before. That is all my Bill aims at, and if we do that we will not meet that question arising under section 92 of the British North America Act. As regards the question of incidental rights, I have also cited cases. In regard to the main proposition, that we are only restoring matters to the position in which they were in law in the various provinces 'before, I would say that that is the position which I endeavoured to take in my argument, and it is a position which the hon. Minister of Justice has not dealt with on this occasion. In Quebec in two cases and in Ontario in two cases it has been decided that owing to the legislation passed by this House the parties cannot recover, and owing to that legislation only. It seems to me that this House is in a position to so modify its own legislation in such a way that provincial law will prevail. I shall not trespass upon the time of the House further, but I am very much disappointed that we cannot have this matter referred to the Committee of the Whole House ; but as no good purpose would be served by dividing Ibe House upon the question, I will not press the question to a division.

In my opinion, it would be unwise to pass such a law. Should this parliament adhere to a legislation of this kind, there would be a matter of conflict between the provincial and federal laws, and that is most assuredly undesirable. In the case of a matter pertaining to provincial jurisdiction that may only incidentally be submitted to this parliament, is it wise to pass legislation that might conflict witli the provincial legislation? I contend it is not. We have this instanced in our statutes in connection with the Insurance Act. In one clause of this Act, it is stipulated that the policy shall not be voided through the insured making an untrue statement in connection with his age. Now, in the jorovince of Quebec, it is provided in our law that such untrue statement is sufficient to cause the insurance contract to be cancelled. Which legislation, one may wonder, is likely to obtain, should an emergencyof this kind come to happen? Jurists are giving their attention to this puzzling question. Why did this parliament interfere in the matter when, under the local legislation, that contract was being cancelled? No available argument has been alleged so far for justifying that interference.
Many lawyers believe that this legislation does not come under the jurisdiction of this parliament because the contracts are subject to the local jurisdiction. Like several judges who have incidentally studied the question, Mr. Holt, in his Treatise on Insurance, believes that this matter is not pertaining to the federal jurisdiction. However, owing to the interference of this parliament, we have a legal conflict of this kind in the province of Quebec, that is we have a provincial law providing that the insurance contract is v'oided in the case of an untrue statement as to the age, and a federal law stating the contrary, which means that the untrue statement does not cause the contract to be cancelled.
It is now suggested that we should have a double legislation in order to regulate the relations as between employers and employees. We would then be in this strange position that, according to the provincial law, the contract is having legal force, whereas our federal legislation would state the contrary. Would it be wise for this parliament to pass such legislation? I submit it would not, and I contend we should not i legislate in such a way as to cause legal conflicts.

speechtext: That Bill (No. 73) to amend the Railway Act (Mr. Lennox) he referred to the Select Standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines.

. Mr. F. B. WADE moved the second reading of Bill (No. 76) to amend the Criminal Code, 1892.
Explain.

I have explained this Bill once before. The Bill is the same as that which I introduced last session. Section 343 of the Criminal Code contains a provision for the punishment of parties who are guilty of stealing gold, quartz, or ores, &c., but the difficulty experienced in the past has been that it was impossible to prove the ownership of the gold or amalgam that was stolen. For instance, a party might trade with the employees of the mine, or they might steal gold or amalgam themselves, and there is no way of identifying it. The mine owners have been labouring under very great hardship in the past. There has been very great complaint throughout the province of Nova Scotia, although I suppose there is scarcely any complaint from the other provinces on account of the difference in character of the gold. In Nova Scotia the complaint is very general that around all the mining camps there are parties who trade in gold, either trading with the workmen or with those

who have an opportunity of breaking the quartz. This has been so ruinous to the mine owners that they determined to take some action, and at the meeting of the Miners' Association of Nova Scotia iast year they adopted a resolution and urged it on the attention of the government. The Bill which was introduced last session did not go through, and they brought it up again in their general meeting. They are unanimous in asking to have this law enacted. I could give very many instances of how the present law works. A party may be in a mining camp, he may be a pedlar, he may be in possession of hundreds and thousands of dollars' worth of gold, and yet it is absolutely impossible to prove he is a thief, because the ownership of the gold cannot be proved. This Bill is designed to remedy that evil by casting the burden of proof on the person who is found in possession of gold or gold amalgam. The Bill does not apply to any other province in the Dominion except Nova Scotia. The provisions of the Bill are taken from the West Australia Act. They are almost identical with what is aimed at here, namely, that on the party who is found in possession of gold or gold amalgam is cast the burden of proof as to how he came by the gold or gold amalgam. I fancy that if this Bill becomes law the stealing that is now going on will be done away with.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time and House went into committee thereon.
On section 343a,

There is in the province of Nova Scotia a feeling that some legislation of this kind should be enacted. I am informed by men who are familiar with the subject, that there have been a great many thefts of gold and a good deal of difficulty in obtaining convictions. I would be inclined to ask, whether the words which concern the burden of proof are not a little too comprehensive.
That is the whole principle of the Bill.
That is the important part of it, I know.

That is what the mine-owners are contending for. If a person comes by the gold honestly he can easily show it, but if he is not able to show that, the presumption is that he came by it dishonestly. I am informed that there are people in cities who deal in an underhand way with parties from these different camps. I have a very strong letter in my possession from Mr. George Stewart, whom the leader of the opposition knows well, saying that this legislation is imperative and that some mines have actually been closed down in consequence of the evil complained of. Near one mining camp in which I was interested, there was a chap who kept a Mr. WADE.
beer shop, and on learning that the yield from the mill was a certain amount, he said : 1 They have beaten me this month by two ounces.' This is a very serious thing, and I hope the leader of the opposition will not object.
I am not objecting.

The matter has been very carefully considered by the Mining Association of Nova Scotia ; I have given it a great deal of thought since last session, and I can see no other way of attempting to remedy the evil.

I agree with the principle of the Bill, but the language is certainly very unrestricted, although I cannot at this moment suggest how you would get at the intention in any different way. Is there any precedent for this legislation in the statutes of the other colonies.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is borrowed almost *word for word from the West Australia Act. I do not think that we should dispose of this Bill to-night. I will have to consider the question of the penalty, and when the matter comes up again I will bring the West Australia Act with me.

If such a law has been enacted elsewhere and has not been accompanied with any injustice or evil results, I do not think I would object to it.
On section 343b,

It seems to me that this section goes very far. Under it, a person absolutely innocent of any crime might be arrested and put to the expense of proving his innocence. The Bill says that any one is guilty of an offence who is deemed ' to have been watching and patrolling outside and in the vicinity of any premises on or about which gold, reasonably suspected of being stolen or unlawfully obtained or held, is found and seized by any peace officer.' It seems to me that it would be important to connect the patrolling and watching with the offence that is really committed ; because a man may be watching and patrolling outside with some other object altogether. He will also be deemed guilty if he is proved ' to have been accompanying any person having in his possession any gold reasonably suspected of being stolen or unlawfully obtained or held.' A person might be in the company of a dishonest man for a perfectly legitimate purpose. He might be in the-company of a man who had really stolen the gold and yet be absolutely innocent of any knowledge of the crime. I quite understand that there is a necessity for some such legislation as that contained in this Bill ; but it seems to me that this sectio.n goes much further than prudent legislation should go. We must be careful, in passing any such legislation, not to expose innocent

persons to the trouble, annoyance and disgrace of being prosecuted on what under other circumstances would be a charge of receiving stolen goods.

So far as I am concerned, X am only seeking to accomplish a certain purpose, and I do not want the Bill to pass this House so framed as to subject any innocent person to improper prosecution. 1 am quite willing that every safeguard should be adopted to prevent that. The proviso in section 343c, to the effect that ' no person shall be convicted of an offence under this section if he proves to the satisfaction of the justice that his presence was innocent, might be extended to the section under discussion. I assume that the hon.: gentleman (Mr. Casgrain) is not familiar with the industry of gold mining in the province Of Nova Scotia. Usually the parties who traffic in stolen gold have confederates. What, is designed here is to prevent a confederate trafficking with miners. Sometimes they go round among the miners with strong waters. The object of this provision is to punish both the man who has the gold in his possession and the man who is in his company at the time it is discovered. This is what the mine owners want. If any safeguard can be thrown about it so that innocent persons will not suffer, I will be content.
I think it should be subject to the qualifications in section 343c, because it makes the guilt of one man depend not upon his own criminal intent, but on the guilt of another.

Let me take the instance stated by the hon. member for Annapolis a moment ago. Suppose a pedlar goes to peddle strong drink to the miners, and is found in company of a man who has stolen gold. It is, I suppose, an offence against the laws of the province to peddle whisky without a license.
They call it 'siwash' around mining camps.

This man would have to admit that he was there selling liquor without a license in order to prove his innocence of the greater offence. Therefore, he would have to admit his guilt, which is against the principles of criminal legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In Nova Scotia he would not be allowed to peddle it with a license.

I would not be troubled much with that consideration, because I do not think he would have any injustice done to him if he were obliged to admit that he was selling liquor. I think we should have, with regard to both these subsections, some such proviso as that contained in 343c, though I do not know that I am perfectly satisfied with the language used.

I am not such a strong temperance advocate as my hon. friend who sits beside me. That was an extreme case ; but a man might be there on other business which he would not wish to divulge, and might be perfectly innocent of complicity in stealing the gold ; but, in order to prove his innocence, he would have to divulge some secret which it would not perhaps be in his interest to divulge. This is going so much against all sound principles of criminal legislation that I think we should proceed with great prudence and so frame the law that innocent persons would not be exposed to the humilation of being charged with this offence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The need of this legislation is very much felt in mining districts. At the close of the discussion we might let the Bill remain in the committee, and have a conference with the Minister of Justice to see if the objections could be met. Of course, care should be taken that no innocent man suffers ; but one only needs to have knowledge of the mining business in Nova Scotia to realize the need of legislation of this kind.
On section 3,
This Act shall apply only to the province of Nova Scotia.

Is- there any other example of criminal legislation being made applicable to one province only ? Rather strange that what should be an offence, and such an offence as theft, in one province, should not be in the others. There are gold mines elsewhere than in Nova Scotia, and if this legislation be proper to apply to Nova Scotia why should it not extend to the whole Dominion ? It is somewhat singular that we should legislate in criminal matters only for one province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have a criminal procedure applicable to Quebec alone.

It would be impossible to make this law applicable to the whole Dominion. How would it operate. in the Yukon, for instance, where gold nuggets are currency ? It would create a revolution out there. I do not know that any evil of the kind exists in the province of Quebec or Ontario. I have heard no complaints, but it applies particularly to Nova Scotia in consequence of the character of its gold. It is a rough heavy gold, and it is very easy for workmen or others to break off these ingots and carry them away. I have seen two pieces of quartz containing $4,000 wrorth of gold, and the man could enrich himself in a very short time by breaking off pieces and carrying them away. I would ask the com-mitteee to allow me to read part of a letter from Mr. George W. Stuart, of Truro, who is one of our foremost gold miners in Nova Scotia, and whom my hon. friend the leader

of the opposition well knows. He is writing to the secretary of the Mfiilng Association :
Will you please state for the next meeting of the council the matter of writing Mr. Wade to press to an immediate finish the amendment of the criminal law in connection with gold stealing.
Only last week one of those peregrinating parasites-an Armenian pedlar-sold no less than 53 ounces of gold here in Truro, procured in the eastern districts. This gold, every grain of it, of course, was stolen from the various mines by the employees, and sold to this miserable wretch of a pedlar at a reduced price, and all manner of trash in the shape of cheap brass jewellery, much of it given in'exchange and any cash that might be received would be spent in raw whisky.
The evil effects of this nefarious business is far-reaching, even to the extent of closing down mines, tying up capital and throwing many men out of employment.	[DOT]
Did we have a law such as we have earnestly asked for, this pilfering would soon cease altogether.
Take the case above referred to, this man (pedlar) would have been arrested and when arrested he would at once plead ignorance of law and give up the gold and every man's name he purchased from, the man who sold to him would be traced to the respective mines they worked in and the gold restored to rightful owners and the miners prosecuted. I trust the council will urge Mr. Wade to introduce this Bill at ojice in the early days of the session ; we are absoutely suffering from want of it.
Then, Mr. Stuart goes on to use even stronger language. I am sure he voices the entire sentiment of the mining industry of Nova Scotia. Further than that, he speaks the opinions of the honest employees in the mines who desire this law to be passed because they are now resting under a suspicion from which they should be relieved.
Progress reported.

On section 1,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that the only change made in the law by this amendment is to make this offense punishable by hard labour and not by imprisonment only. The disadvantage of the present law is that it is found that when it becomes too cold to stay outside, the prisons fill up by the influx of those who break this law, thus causing expense and injury to the public. But, under this proposed amendment, the person guilty of infraction of the law would be called upon to do something for his country in the way of hard labour.
And then you will let them out on ticket-of-leave.

Mr. .1. E. ARMSTRONG. I would like to request the government that all petitions, pro and con, with reference to the duty on oil be laid on the table. A number of petitions have been presented to the government from towns and villages In western Ontario asking the government not to interfere with the duty, on oil, and there have been one or two asking that the duty be interfered with. 1 would ask that all the petitions he laid on the table.

Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to make a personal explanation. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice a short time ago said that a reference had been made of the telephone question to the Supreme Court. I put a question on the paper asking whether a reference had been made, and if so, what reference. The answer given by the Minister of Railways was that no reference had been made. I take this opportunity of letting the public, and especially those directly interested, know that no reference has been made to the Supreme Court, and that the Minister of Justice was in error when he made the statement he did. I also take tills opportunity of informing the government that In the Railway Committee an arrangement was made that certain amendments of mine to the Railway Act should be considered in committee two weeks hence, and I wish to take this opportunity of informing the government that that arrangement does not preclude my bringing forward my amendments in connection with the Bill of the Minister of Justice to amend the Railway Act.
